name: The Soviet crewed Mars programme
short_status: Cancelled, and never built. Design ran at OKB-1 from 1959, was halted by decree on 13 May 1961, continued anyway, was revived in 1969 as Aelita and died with the N1; the only hardware was a Moscow mock-up.

facts.label: What this covers
facts.value: Soviet studies of a crewed flight to Mars, from the first sketches at OKB-1 in 1959 to the closure of the N1 rocket in the 1970s. The main threads are the Martian Piloted Complex (МПК) under Mikhail Tikhonravov, the Heavy Interplanetary Ship (ТМК, Тяжёлый межпланетный корабль) in the Maksimov and Feoktistov variants, the Mars and Venus flyby theme МАВР, and the 1969 programme code-named Аэлита (Aelita) with its Mars Expeditionary Complex (МЭК). None of it flew.

facts.label: Where the work was done
facts.value: OKB-1, Korolev's bureau at Podlipki, later TsKBEM and today RKK Energia. Bugrov and Evtifyev both place the origin in department 9 under Mikhail Tikhonravov, with a sector under Gleb Maksimov and a sector under Konstantin Feoktistov. Anatoly Zak's RussianSpaceWeb and Mark Wade's Encyclopedia Astronautica instead say Section or Department 3. From 1966 the research institute NII-88, later TsNIIMash, ran its own parallel Mars studies, and from 1969 Vladimir Chelomei's TsKBM and Mikhail Yangel's bureau were brought in.

facts.label: The founding decrees
facts.value: Central Committee and Council of Ministers decrees No. 714-295 and No. 715-296 of 23 June 1960. Bugrov, who worked on the project, gives the title of 715-296 as "On the creation of powerful launch vehicles, satellites, spacecraft and the mastery of space in 1960-1967" and says it called for a rocket system of 1,000 to 2,000 tonnes launch mass able to place a heavy interplanetary ship of 60 to 80 tonnes into Earth orbit. The magazine Ogonyok states that the same decree fixed the departure date.

facts.label: The departure date
facts.value: 8 June 1971, chosen from the Mars launch window at the favourable opposition of that year. The return date is published two ways. Encyclopedia Astronautica and Russian Wikipedia give 10 July 1974; Ogonyok gives 10 June 1974. Wade also states the voyage lasted three years, one month and two days, which from 8 June 1971 arrives at 10 July 1974 and not 10 June, so the arithmetic favours July. We have not seen the decree text itself and treat the return date as unsettled.

facts.label: MPK, the first complex
facts.value: Tikhonravov's Martian Piloted Complex would have been assembled in low Earth orbit and flown to Mars on ordinary chemical propellants, entered Mars orbit, landed a crew and brought back a small capsule. Published figures disagree. Igor Afanasyev gives about 1,630 tonnes, 20 to 25 N1 launches, an expedition of more than 2.5 years and 15 tonnes returning. Wade repeats 1,630 tonnes and 20 to 25 launches, then tabulates 1,360 tonnes in low Earth orbit, 900 days total, a crew of six and a year on the surface. Zheleznyakov gives about 1,600 tonnes, not fewer than 20 launches, and a four-year expedition with roughly two years at the planet. Wade dates the MPK study to 1956, which sits oddly with the Russian accounts that date the Mars work to 1959; Wade himself notes that Korolev, defending the N1 draft project in July 1962, said he had first sketched the rocket in 1956 to 1957 to support a large crewed Mars expedition. Bugrov, who worked inside the project, describes a far smaller complex once the configuration settled in 1964: 400 to 500 tonnes, later 500 to 600, assembled from 75-tonne blocks in four to six N1 launches.

facts.label: TMK-1, the Maksimov ship
facts.value: A three-person flyby ship of about 75 tonnes, to be launched by one N1 and pushed onto a Mars trajectory by a liquid oxygen and kerosene stage, which would have left 30 tonnes on the coast. After 10.5 months it would pass Mars, drop automatic landers and let Mars gravity bend it back towards Earth. Wade gives it 12 m in length and 6 m across the crew section, with a habitation, work, biological and equipment section, an airlock, a solar storm shelter and a re-entry capsule. Wade dates the completion of the draft project (эскизный проект) to 12 October 1961.

facts.label: TMK-E, the Feoktistov ship
facts.value: Feoktistov's group judged a single-launch flyby too limited and proposed a full landing expedition assembled in orbit and driven by ion engines powered by a nuclear reactor. Leonid Gorshkov, who was in that group, records a 7 MW reactor and a crew of six in the 1960 version. Wade gives the engine design as 7.5 kgf of thrust at a predicted specific impulse of 10,000 seconds, which would have meant a spiral departure lasting months, and says solar power for the same engines would have needed roughly 36,000 square metres of panel, which is why the reactor was chosen. Zheleznyakov writes that Korolev kept the theory and the layout work in house and handed development of the reactor itself to Vasily Grabin's TsNII-58, then building experimental fast-neutron reactors. None of the three figures in this paragraph comes from Gorshkov.

facts.label: The Mars Train
facts.value: The TMK-E surface plan was a train of five separately landed wagons: a crew cabin with manipulators and a drill, a platform for a convertiplane to fly in the Martian atmosphere, two rocket launch platforms carrying a main and a spare ascent vehicle, and a nuclear reactor wagon to power the whole thing. Wade gives the landers as conical aeroshells 5.5 m across and 9 m high at about 10 tonnes each. Gorshkov describes the train crossing the planet from one pole to the other. In the 1969 rework the reactor went to 15 MW, three reactors replaced one, the landers were cut from five to one and the crew from six to four.

facts.label: The 13 May 1961 cancellation
facts.value: Decree No. 420-174 of the Central Committee and the Council of Ministers, "On the revision of plans for space objects towards the fulfilment of tasks of defence significance". Its stated purpose is to concentrate resources and design bureau effort first of all on tasks connected with the defence of the country. Point 1(v) orders a halt to development of the heavy interplanetary ship for flight to Mars and Venus, referring to it by that description and citing decree 715-296. Point 1(d) halts work on preparing expeditions to the surface of the Moon, Mars and Venus. Point 1(z) pushes the N1 rocket back to 1965. We read the Roscosmos scan of the signed document; it carries no text layer, so the wording here is our translation of the page image. The decree stopped less than it says: Maksimov's draft project was completed on 12 October 1961, five months later, and Bugrov describes design and test work running on to 1974 and 1975.

facts.label: MAVR, and which MAVR
facts.value: Two different projects carry this name and English sources merge them. Wade and Zheleznyakov describe МАВР as a 1963 variation of Maksimov's OKB-1 flyby ship adding a Venus pass, at 75 tonnes with a crew of three, and read the name as MArs plus VeneRa. Mikhail Evtifyev, writing about work at TsNIIMash, describes МАВР as a theme assigned there in early June 1966 to department 12 under Golovin, sector Yevich, group Pronin, and reads the name as "Марс, Венера - разом", Mars and Venus at once. His MAVR has a crew of six, an Earth to Mars to Venus to Earth trajectory, a 1975 departure, a flight of 480 to 600 days and an initial mass of 105,680 kg.

facts.label: What MAVR carried
facts.value: In the TsNIIMash version: a universal habitation block 6 m across divided into five or six decks with six private cabins, a saloon, a greenhouse, a galley, a bathroom, a laboratory, a workshop, a radiation shelter and an airlock; a detachable astronomy block about 7 m long with a telescope and an observer's cabin; separate spherical probes to be dropped at Mars and at Venus; and a 30 square metre parabolic solar concentrator that would have fed the 14 square metre greenhouse through a Fresnel mirror and doubled as the dish for the deep space radio link. Permanent artificial gravity by rotation was rejected in favour of a centrifuge used periodically. The report was approved by TsNIIMash director Yuri Mozzhorin on 12 July 1968.

facts.label: The year in the mock-up
facts.value: The hardware that did get built was a ground analogue of the TMK habitation section, the experimental rig ЭУ-37, assembled in 1967 to 1969 inside the Ground Experimental Complex or НЭК at the Institute of Medico-Biological Problems in Moscow. Bugrov is explicit that the НЭК was the facility and the TMK mock-up was mounted inside it. The two were not the same thing. Three testers, the physician German Manovtsev, the biologist Andrei Bozhko and the technician Boris Ulybyshev, lived sealed inside it for a year, recycling their own air and water and growing greens in a small greenhouse. Bugrov dates the end of the run to 5 November 1968; Russian accounts give the start as 5 November 1967 and the length as 366 days. Wade instead dates the start to 5 March 1967, which does not match the Russian record. Bozhko later wrote a book about it, "Год в Звездолёте" (A Year in the Starship, 1975).

facts.label: Order No. 232, the contested authorisation
facts.value: The 1969 re-authorisation is the spine of the Aelita story and its date, number and content are all disputed. Boris Chertok, who was in the room for the meetings that led to it, writes that on 30 June the minister issued an order obliging Chelomei to produce within one year a Mars complex design based on the UR-700M or UR-900 rocket and the MK-700M ship. He gives no number. Wade gives "decree 232 of 30 June 1969", attributes it to the Ministry of Defence, and says the technical specification was written by TsNIIMash and NIITI and the project code-named Aelita; Zak gives 30 June 1969 and No. 232 and follows Chertok in aiming it at Chelomei. Evtifyev, who worked on the TsNIIMash side, writes that on 30 July 1969 Order No. 232 of the Minister of General Machine Building appeared, on development of a rocket and space complex to provide an expedition to the planet Mars, project code Aelita. The ministry in question was General Machine Building, headed by Sergei Afanasyev from 1965 to 1983. Wade's Ministry of Defence is the wrong one.

facts.label: MEK, the OKB-1 answer to Aelita
facts.value: Mishin had signed off the advance project for an uprated N1M rocket on 28 May 1969, and Feoktistov's group designed the Mars Expeditionary Complex to use it. Afanasyev and Zheleznyakov give 630 days total, 30 days in Mars orbit and 5 days on the surface for three of the crew; Wade gives the same but with five to seven surface days and a crew of three to six. Wade puts it at 175 m long, 17 m span, 150 tonnes, with two YaE-2 reactors totalling 15,000 kW cooled by liquid lithium, 6.2 kgf of thrust at 8,000 seconds specific impulse, a 20-tonne lander 11 m across and a 10-tonne return capsule with a 6 m lens-shaped base shield. Assembly is described as two launches of about 75 tonnes each, by Wade explicitly on the N1M and by Zheleznyakov on the N1, but Afanasyev writes of two unmanned blocks of about 150 tonnes each, twice the total.

facts.label: The landing complex that shrank
facts.value: Under Aelita, TsNIIMash worked the Mars surface complex down a ladder of decreasing ambition. The heaviest, at 122 tonnes, was a three-wagon six-wheeled train for three people, thirty days of driving at about 12 km/h over a planned 1,500 km route, with a Romashka-type 100 kW reactor in the rear wagon, to be shielded by Martian soil augered into a hollow container. Below it came a 95-tonne two-part variant, an 80-tonne version with a fixed laboratory and a wheeled buggy of 20 km range, a 45-tonne version cut to seven days and 5 km, and finally a 23-tonne "priority" complex for two people and four days, of which Evtifyev writes that almost no scientific return was expected and its task was to plant a flag on the surface of Mars.

facts.label: How it ended
facts.value: By the end of 1969, Wade writes, Mishin and Yangel had dropped out of the competition, leaving Chelomei. Wade records that a government expert commission reviewed his UR-700M and MK-700 draft project in 1972 and, on the grounds that it needed decades of development and tens of billions of roubles, recommended deferring crewed Mars expeditions indefinitely. On 23 November 1972 the fourth and last N1 failed; Evtifyev writes that this buried both MAVR and Aelita. A government decree of 21 May 1974 replaced Mishin with Valentin Glushko at the head of the new NPO Energia, and on 24 June, after the N1's chief designer Boris Dorofeyev refused to draft it, Glushko wrote and signed the order stopping work on the N1 himself. Chertok records that Glushko's order was backed by neither an order of the minister nor a decision of the Military Industrial Commission, and that the formal Central Committee and Council of Ministers decision to end N1-L3 and write off the money came only in February 1976, and that 6 billion roubles were written off.

timeline: Central Committee and Council of Ministers decrees 714-295 and 715-296 authorise a rocket system of 1,000 to 2,000 tonnes able to lift a 60 to 80 tonne interplanetary ship. Ogonyok reports that the same decision fixed the departure for Mars at 8 June 1971.

Decree 420-174 orders a halt to development of the heavy interplanetary ship for Mars and Venus, a halt to preparation of expeditions to the surfaces of the Moon, Mars and Venus, and a slip of the N1 rocket to 1965. The stated reason is concentration of resources on defence tasks. Eleven months after the programme was authorised, it is cancelled by name.
The draft project for Maksimov's three-person flyby ship is completed anyway, five months after the cancellation. Work continues inside the bureau without a government mandate behind it.

The last OKB-1 iteration of the design, known as KK, the space complex for delivering a piloted expedition to Mars, is finished. Four mission profiles are traded, and the orbital-descent scheme is preferred. Then N1-L3 and the Moon absorb the bureau.
NII-88, later TsNIIMash, is told to study the OKB-1 flyby ship and produce its own advance project for a crewed flyby of two planets. The theme is given the code МАВР, for Mars and Venus at once.

Manovtsev, Bozhko and Ulybyshev spend a year sealed in the ground analogue of the TMK habitation section in Moscow, on regenerated air and water. Bugrov records that everything except food was recycled by physical and chemical means, with a greenhouse of Khibiny cabbage, borage, cress and dill supplying vitamins and fibre.
TsNIIMash director Yuri Mozzhorin signs off the MAVR report, the product of design research running from 1966 to 1968 on crewed complexes for an expedition flying past Mars and Venus.

At a council of chief designers, Keldysh says the lunar landing should be slipped to 1972 and asks whether Mars would not be the better goal. Chertok records him saying "I am for Mars" and proposing that two N1 launches with a docking in orbit could place a crewed Mars satellite in 1975.

At a meeting in Mishin's office, the former office of Korolev, Mishin describes the Mars expedition to the assembled ministers and Party officials. Chertok records that the report was heard without enthusiasm and that only Keldysh spoke for continuing, and then only if it did not damage the lunar programme.

The order that started Aelita. Chertok dates it 30 June and describes it as obliging Chelomei to design a Mars complex on the UR-700M or UR-900 within a year; Wade and Zak give the number 232 and the same date; Evtifyev dates Order No. 232 of the Minister of General Machine Building to 30 July and describes it as covering a rocket and space complex for an expedition to Mars under the code name Aelita. Three bureaus begin competing.

The fourth N1 fails. Evtifyev writes that the theme was closed and the hopes for MAVR and Aelita were buried with it. Wade records that a government expert commission had already reviewed Chelomei's UR-700M and MK-700 draft project that year and recommended putting crewed Mars expeditions off indefinitely.

A government decree of 21 May 1974 makes Valentin Glushko general designer and director of the new NPO Energia in Mishin's place. On 24 June, after the N1's chief designer Boris Dorofeyev refuses to draft it, Glushko writes and signs the order stopping work on the N1 himself. Chertok notes that the order was backed by neither an order of the minister nor a decision of the Military Industrial Commission.

The Central Committee and Council of Ministers formally end N1-L3 and write off the spending, 6 billion roubles in the prices of the day. A decree of 17 February 1976 creating the reusable system that became Energia and Buran closes the matter.
